docs.title: 📘 1. Introduction to Electrochemistry
docs.text: Electrochemistry deals with the relationship between electrical energy and chemical energy — specifically, the study of redox reactions that involve this interconversion.

docs.title: Key Concepts:
docs.text:
• Electrolysis = Chemical energy is created from electrical energy (using electricity to cause a redox reaction)
  • Electrochemical Cell = Electrical energy is created by converting chemical energy (a redox process produces electrical energy)

docs.title: 📗 2. Electrolytes
docs.text: An electrolyte is a substance that conducts electricity when dissolved in water (or in molten state) by producing ions.

docs.title: Classification of Electrolytes
docs.text: Type Description Examples Strong Electrolytes Completely dissociates into ions in water NaCl, KCl, HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ Weak Electrolytes Partially dissociates/ionizes into ions CH₃COOH, NH₄OH, NH₃, H₂CO₃ Non-Electrolytes Does not conduct electric current in molten state or aqueous solution Urea, Glucose, Ethanol

docs.title: Dissociation Example:
docs.text:
NaCl (aq) → Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
H₂O → H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)

docs.title: 📙 3. Difference Between Electrolyte and Electrochemistry
docs.text: Property Electrolyte Electrochemistry Definition A substance that conducts electricity when dissolved in water A system/reaction involving the relationship between electrical and chemical energy Energy Conversion Chemical energy is created from electric energy Electric energy is created by converting chemical energy Process Type Using electricity causes a redox reaction A redox process produces electrical energy Focus The conducting medium itself The entire system of electrical-chemical interconversion

docs.title: 📕 4. Electrodes
docs.text: Electrodes are metallic rods dipped into the electrolyte through which electricity enters or leaves the electrolyte.

docs.title: Two Types of Electrodes:
docs.text: Electrode Type of Reaction Charge Function Anode Oxidation Positive (+) Electrons leave; loss of electrons Cathode Reduction Negative (−) Electrons enter; gain of electrons

docs.title: 🔑 Memory Trick:
docs.text:
• Oxidation = Loss of electrons (Anode)
  • Reduction = Gain of electrons (Cathode)
  • "An Ox, Red Cat" → Anode Oxidation, Reduction Cathode

docs.title: A) Electrolysis of Water (H₂O)
docs.text:
At Cathode (Reduction): $\(2H^+ + 2e^- \rightarrow H_2 \uparrow\)$

At Anode (Oxidation): $\(2OH^- \rightarrow H_2O + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 + 2e^-\)$

docs.title: B) Electrolysis of Aqueous NaCl Solution
docs.text:
Dissociation: $\(NaCl \rightarrow Na^+ + Cl^-\)$

At Cathode (Reduction): $\(Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na \text{ (Sodium deposited at cathode)}\)$

At Anode (Oxidation): $\(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 \uparrow + 2e^- \text{ (Cl₂ gas released at anode)}\)$

docs.title: C) Electrolysis of Molten NaCl
docs.text:
Dissociation: $\(NaCl (l) \rightarrow Na^+ + Cl^-\)$

At Cathode: $\(Na^+ + e^- \rightarrow Na\)$

At Anode:$\(2Cl^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\)$

docs.title: 🔬 Faraday's First Law
docs.text:
The mass of a substance deposited or liberated at any electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

Mathematical Form: $\(W \propto Q\)$ $\(W = ZQ\)$

Where: - W = Mass of substance deposited (grams) - Q = Quantity of electricity (Coulombs) - Z = Electrochemical equivalent (g/C)

Also: $\(Q = I \times t\)$

Where: - I = Current (Amperes) - t = Time (seconds)

Relation: $\(Z = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{E}{F}\)$

Where: - E = Equivalent weight - F = Faraday constant = 96,500 C

docs.title: 🔬 Faraday's Second Law
docs.text:
When the same quantity of electricity is passed through different electrolytic solutions connected in series, the ratio of the weights of different substances deposited at different electrodes is equal to the ratio of their equivalent weights.

Mathematical Form: $\(\frac{W_1}{W_2} = \frac{E_1}{E_2}\)$

Where: - W₁, W₂ = Weights of substances deposited - E₁, E₂ = Equivalent weights of the substances

Derivation: $\(\because W_1 = Z_1 \times Q \quad \text{and} \quad W_2 = Z_2 \times Q\)$

\[\therefore \frac{W_1}{W_2} = \frac{Z_1}{Z_2} = \frac{E_1}{E_2} \quad (\text{since } Z \propto E)\]

docs.title: 🔋 7. Faraday Constant (F)
docs.text: Definition: The charge carried by 1 mole of electrons is called 1 Faraday.

docs.title: Calculation:
docs.text:
• Charge of 1 electron = \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) Coulombs
  • 1 mole of electrons = \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) electrons

Charge of 1 mole of electrons: $\(F = 6.022 \times 10^{23} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\)$ $\(F = 96{,}368 \text{ C} \approx 96{,}500 \text{ C}\)$

\[\boxed{F = 96{,}500 \text{ Coulombs} = 1 \text{ Faraday}}\]

docs.title: Formula:
docs.text: \[\text{Equivalent Weight (E)} = \frac{\text{Atomic Weight (or Molecular Weight)}}{\text{Valency (n-factor)}}\]

docs.title: 📌 Problem 1: Electrochemical Equivalent of Ag
docs.text:
Question: When 3 amperes of electric current is passed for 20 minutes through a AgNO₃ solution, 4 g of Ag is deposited. Calculate the electrochemical equivalent (Z) of Ag.

Given: - Current (I) = 3 A - Time (t) = 20 min = 1200 s - Mass deposited (W) = 4 g

Solution:

Using Q = I × t: $\(Q = 3 \times 1200 = 3600 \text{ C}\)$

Using Faraday's First Law: W = ZQ $\(4 = Z \times 3600\)$ $\(Z = \frac{4}{3600} = \frac{1}{900} \text{ g/C}\)$

\[\boxed{Z = 1.11 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g/C} \approx 0.001 \text{ g/C}}\]

docs.title: 📌 Problem 2: Mass of Silver Deposited
docs.text:
Question: What amount of silver (Ag) will be deposited when an electric current of 2.1 A is passed through a AgNO₃ solution for 20 minutes? (Atomic weight of Ag = 108 a.m.u.)

Given: - Current (I) = 2.1 A - Time (t) = 20 min = 1200 s - Atomic weight of Ag = 108 - Valency = 1 → Equivalent weight (E) = 108 - Faraday constant (F) = 96,500 C

Solution:

Step 1: Calculate the charge (Q) $\(Q = I \times t = 2.1 \times 1200 = 2520 \text{ C}\)$

Step 2: Use the formula $\(W = \frac{1}{F} \times E \times Q\)$ $\(W = \frac{1}{96500} \times 108 \times 2520\)$ $\(\boxed{W = 2.82 \text{ g of Ag}}\)$

docs.title: 📌 Problem 3: Charge Required for Conversion
docs.text:
Question: How many coulombs of charge are required for the following conversion: $\(Cr^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow Cr(s) \text{ for 2 moles of electrons}\)$

Solution:

The reaction is: $\(Cr^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cr(s)\)$

For 2 moles of electrons, the charge required is: $\(Q = n \times F = 2 \times 96{,}500\)$

\[\boxed{Q = 1{,}93{,}000 \text{ C} = 2 \text{ Faraday}}\]

docs.title: Detailed Study Notes: Fuels, Classification, and Combustion
1. Definition of Fuel
docs.text: • Fuel: Any material that can react to release chemical or nuclear energy as heat or to be used to perform work.

docs.title: 2. Classification of Fuels
docs.text: Fuels are broadly categorized based on their physical state, origin, and method of energy production.

docs.title: A. Solid Fuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Solid materials burnt to produce energy and provide heating via combustion.
  • Examples: Coke, charcoal.

docs.title: B. Liquid Fuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Combustible or energy-generating liquid molecules used to create mechanical/kinetic energy.
  • Key Characteristic: The fumes of liquid fuels are flammable, not the liquid fluid itself.
  • Origin: Most liquid fuels are derived from fossilized remains of dead plants and animals exposed to extreme heat and pressure within the Earth's crust.
  • Examples: Diesel, gasoline, kerosene, LPG, coal tar, naphtha, ethanol.

docs.title: C. Gaseous Fuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Fuels that exist as gases under ordinary conditions.
  • Composition: Composed primarily of hydrocarbons (e.g., methane, propane), hydrogen, carbon monoxide, or mixtures thereof.
  • Advantages: Easily transmitted and distributed via pipes from origin directly to consumption points.
  • Examples: Hydrogen, propane, methane, coal gas, water gas, blast furnace gas, coke oven gas, Compressed Natural Gas (CNG).

docs.title: D. Biofuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Solid, liquid, or gaseous fuels consisting of or derived from renewable biomass.
  • Origin: Produced from rapidly replenishable carbon sources such as plants and plant-derived materials.
  • Examples: Bioethanol, biodiesel, direct biomass fuel.

docs.title: E. Fossil Fuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Hydrocarbons formed over hundreds of millions of years from ancient plant and animal remains subjected to high heat and pressure in the absence of oxygen.
  • Composition: High percentage of carbon content.
  • Examples: Coal, petroleum (liquid petroleum), natural gas.

docs.title: F. Nuclear Fuels
docs.text:
• Definition: Materials used to derive nuclear energy through nuclear reactions .
  • Fissile Nuclear Fuels: \(^{235} \text{U}\) (Uranium-235) and \(^{239} \text{Pu}\) (Plutonium-239), which undergo nuclear fission chain reactions in nuclear reactors.
  • Fusion Fuels: Nuclear fusion serves as the main fuel source for stars (currently not commercially utilized by humans).

docs.title: 3. Combustion of Fuels
docs.text: • Definition: High-temperature exothermic redox chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidant (typically atmospheric oxygen), yielding oxidized gaseous products (smoke).

docs.title: Stoichiometric Combustion Equation for Hydrocarbons
docs.text:
For a general hydrocarbon \(C_xH_y\):

\(C_xH_y + zO_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \frac{y}{2}H_2O\) where: $$ z = x + \frac{1}{4}y $$

docs.title: Example: Burning of Propane (\(C_3H_8\))
docs.text: \[ C_3H_8 + 5O_2  \rightarrow  3CO_2 + 4H_2O \]

docs.title: 4. Calorific Value
docs.text:
• Calorific Value of Fuel: Total amount of energy released by the complete combustion of a unit mass/volume of fuel.
  • Units: Energy per unit mass/volume (e.g., \(\text{kJ/kg}\) or \(\text{Btu/lb}\)) .
  • Calorific Value of Food: Energy available from food upon digestion (primarily from carbohydrates and fats) .

docs.title: Types of Calorific Value
docs.text:
1. Higher Calorific Value (HCV) / Gross Calorific Value (GCV) / Higher Heating Value (HHV):
  2. Assumes that the water produced during combustion is completely condensed .

  3. The latent heat contained in the water vapor is recovered .

  4. Lower Calorific Value (LCV) / Net Calorific Value (NCV) / Lower Heating Value (LHV):

  5. Products of combustion contain water vapor that is allowed to escape .
  6. The latent heat contained in the water vapor is not recovered [cite: 1].

docs.title: 6. Properties of an Ideal Fuel
docs.text: An ideal fuel should possess the following characteristics: * High Calorific Value: Yields maximum heat per unit mass [cite: 1]. * Moderate Ignition Temperature: Easily ignited, but not unsafe to store/handle [cite: 1]. * Low Moisture Content: Minimizes energy lost in evaporating water [cite: 1]. * Low Non-Combustible Matter Content: Minimal ash or residue generation [cite: 1]. * Non-Harmful Combustion Products: Environmentally safe, minimal toxic emissions (\(NO_x\), \(SO_x\), etc.) [cite: 1]. * Low Cost: Economically viable [cite: 1]. * Easy and Safe to Transport & Store: Convenient handling logistics [cite: 1].

docs.title: 1. Definition & Overview
docs.text:
• Lubricant: A substance (usually organic) introduced to reduce friction between surfaces in mutual contact, thereby reducing the heat generated when surfaces move.

  • Additional functions include transmitting forces, transporting foreign particles, and heating or cooling surfaces.

  • Lubricity: The property of reducing friction.

  • Lubrication: The process or technique of using a lubricant to reduce friction and wear and tear in contact between two surfaces.
  • Applications:
  • Industrial: To ensure proper, efficient functioning of mechanisms and reduce wear.
  • Non-Industrial: Cooking (oils/fats to prevent food sticking), bioapplications (artificial joints), ultrasound examinations, and medical examinations.

docs.title: 2. Properties of Ideal Lubricants
docs.text:
A high-quality lubricant generally exhibits the following characteristics:

  • High boiling point and low freezing point (remains liquid over a wide temperature range)
  • High Viscosity Index
  • Thermal stability
  • Hydraulic stability
  • Demulsibility
  • Corrosion prevention
  • High resistance to oxidation

docs.title: 3. Lubricant Additives
docs.text:
Modern automotive lubricants contain as many as 10 additives, comprising up to 20% of the overall lubricant composition.

Additive Primary Function Common Examples / Notes Anti-foaming Agents Increase surface tension to prevent foam formation. Silicone compounds Viscosity Index Improvers Help lubricants maintain viscosity at high temperatures. Polyacrylates, butadiene Antioxidants / Metal Deactivators Suppress oxidative degradation of hydrocarbon molecules. • Free radical inhibitors (e.g., BHT / butylated hydroxytoluene) for low temperatures• Dithiophosphates for \(T > 90^{\circ}\text{C}\) where metals catalyze oxidation Detergents Keep engine components clean by preventing high-temperature deposit formation. — Corrosion Inhibitors Alkaline materials that absorb acids to prevent metal parts from corroding/rusting. Alkylsulfonate salts Anti-wear Additives Form protective "tribofilms" on metal parts to suppress wear. Phosphate esters, zinc dithiophosphates

  • Aromatic

docs.text:

  • Polyalpha-olefin (PAO)
  • Synthetic esters

  • Phosphate esters
  • Alkylated naphthalenes (AN)
  • Silicate esters
  • Ionic fluids
  • Multiply alkylated cyclopentanes (MAC)

docs.title: C. Solid Lubricants
docs.text:
• PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene): Chemically inert coating layer used in cooking utensils (non-stick) and as an additive in special greases; stable up to \(350^{\circ}\text{C}\).
  • Inorganic Solids: Graphite, hexagonal boron nitride, molybdenum disulfide (\(\text{MoS}_2\)), and tungsten disulfide (\(\text{WS}_2\)).
  • Metals & Alloys: Pure metals, metal alloys, and composites used as grease additives or sole constituents of bearings/sliding surfaces.

docs.title: D. Aqueous Lubrication
docs.text: • Utilizes liquid-solid interfaces; strongly hydrated brush polymers such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) serve as lubricants in various technological applications.

docs.title: E. Biolubricants
docs.text:
• Derived from vegetable oils and renewable plant/animal sources.
  • Primarily composed of triglyceride esters.

docs.title: F. Gas Lubricants
docs.text:
• Gases like nitrogen and helium are used as lubricants.
  • Key Advantages: Wide operating temperature range, extremely low friction (due to low viscosity), zero vaporization, zero solidification, and no thermal decomposition.

docs.title: 5. Main Functions of Lubricants
docs.text:
1. Keep Moving Parts Apart: Creates a physical barrier (thin fluid film) between moving parts to reduce friction, wear, surface fatigue, heat, operating noise, and vibration.
  2. Reduce Friction: Lower lubricant-to-surface friction reduces overall system friction, resulting in decreased wear particles, less heat generation, and improved efficiency.
  3. Heat Transfer: Liquid lubricants absorb and carry away heat efficiently due to their high specific heat capacity through continuous circulation to cooler parts.
  4. Transport Contaminants & Debris: Circulating lubricants carry debris and contaminants to filters. Detergents and dispersants assist in keeping debris suspended for removal.
  5. Transmit Power: Used as hydraulic fluid in hydrostatic power transmission (accounts for a large portion of global lubricant production) and automatic transmission torque converters.
  6. Protect Against Wear: Prevents mechanical wear via physical separation and anti-wear/extreme pressure additives.
  7. Prevent Corrosion: Chemical additives exclude moisture and bond to metallic surfaces, mitigating surface corrosion and rust.
  8. Gas Sealing: Fills microscopic gaps/clearances between moving parts via capillary action (e.g., sealing engine pistons and shafts).# Unit: Lubricants

  • Non-Industrial: Cooking (oils/fats to prevent food sticking), bioapplications (artificial joints), ultrasound examinations, and medical examinations.

docs.title: 2. Properties of Ideal Lubricants
docs.text:
A high-quality lubricant generally exhibits the following characteristics:

  • High boiling point and low freezing point (remains liquid over a wide temperature range)
  • High Viscosity Index
  • Thermal stability
  • Hydraulic stability
  • Demulsibility
  • Corrosion prevention
  • High resistance to oxidation

docs.title: 3. Lubricant Additives
docs.text:
Modern automotive lubricants contain as many as 10 additives, comprising up to 20% of the overall lubricant composition.

Additive Primary Function Common Examples / Notes Anti-foaming Agents Increase surface tension to prevent foam formation. Silicone compounds Viscosity Index Improvers Help lubricants maintain viscosity at high temperatures. Polyacrylates, butadiene Antioxidants / Metal Deactivators Suppress oxidative degradation of hydrocarbon molecules. • Free radical inhibitors (e.g., BHT / butylated hydroxytoluene) for low temperatures

• Dithiophosphates for \(T > 90^{\circ}\text{C}\) where metals catalyze oxidation | | Detergents | Keep engine components clean by preventing high-temperature deposit formation. | — | | Corrosion Inhibitors | Alkaline materials that absorb acids to prevent metal parts from corroding/rusting. | Alkylsulfonate salts | | Anti-wear Additives | Form protective "tribofilms" on metal parts to suppress wear. | Phosphate esters, zinc dithiophosphates |

docs.title: A. Mineral Oils
docs.text:
Base oils derived from crude oil, categorized by their prevailing chemical composition:

  • Paraffinic
  • Naphthenic
  • Aromatic

docs.title: B. Synthetic Oils
docs.text:
Synthetic hydrocarbon lubricants produced from petroleum derivatives, including:

  • Polyalpha-olefin (PAO)
  • Synthetic esters
  • Polyalkylene glycols (PAG)
  • Phosphate esters
  • Alkylated naphthalenes (AN)
  • Silicate esters
  • Ionic fluids
  • Multiply alkylated cyclopentanes (MAC)

docs.title: C. Solid Lubricants
docs.text:
• PTFE (Polytetrafluoroethylene): Chemically inert coating layer used in cooking utensils (non-stick) and as an additive in special greases; stable up to \(350^{\circ}\text{C}\).
  • Inorganic Solids: Graphite, hexagonal boron nitride, molybdenum disulfide (\(\text{MoS}_2\)), and tungsten disulfide (\(\text{WS}_2\)).
  • Metals & Alloys: Pure metals, metal alloys, and composites used as grease additives or sole constituents of bearings/sliding surfaces.

docs.title: D. Aqueous Lubrication
docs.text: • Utilizes liquid-solid interfaces; strongly hydrated brush polymers such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) serve as lubricants in various technological applications.

docs.title: E. Biolubricants
docs.text:
• Derived from vegetable oils and renewable plant/animal sources.
  • Primarily composed of triglyceride esters.

docs.title: F. Gas Lubricants
docs.text:
• Gases like nitrogen and helium are used as lubricants.
  • Key Advantages: Wide operating temperature range, extremely low friction (due to low viscosity), zero vaporization, zero solidification, and no thermal decomposition.

docs.title: 5. Main Functions of Lubricants
docs.text:
1. Keep Moving Parts Apart: Creates a physical barrier (thin fluid film) between moving parts to reduce friction, wear, surface fatigue, heat, operating noise, and vibration.
  2. Reduce Friction: Lower lubricant-to-surface friction reduces overall system friction, resulting in decreased wear particles, less heat generation, and improved efficiency.
  3. Heat Transfer: Liquid lubricants absorb and carry away heat efficiently due to their high specific heat capacity through continuous circulation to cooler parts.
  4. Transport Contaminants & Debris: Circulating lubricants carry debris and contaminants to filters. Detergents and dispersants assist in keeping debris suspended for removal.
  5. Transmit Power: Used as hydraulic fluid in hydrostatic power transmission (accounts for a large portion of global lubricant production) and automatic transmission torque converters.
  6. Protect Against Wear: Prevents mechanical wear via physical separation and anti-wear/extreme pressure additives.
  7. Prevent Corrosion: Chemical additives exclude moisture and bond to metallic surfaces, mitigating surface corrosion and rust.
  8. Gas Sealing: Fills microscopic gaps/clearances between moving parts via capillary action (e.g., sealing engine pistons and shafts).# Unit: Lubricants

Aim:- To identify the common laboratory apparatus.

(i) Test Tube:- These are small glass tube closed at one end. Test tubes are generally made of glass, some are also made of pyrex or corning glass. These are available in various sizes and are used for carrying out different tests.

(ii) Beaker:- These are flat bottomed cylindrical vessel with a beak made of pyrex or corning glass. They are available in different sizes ranging from 50 ml to 1 L. These are used for storing liquids and solutions for performing different experiments.

(iii) Funnel:- These are coned shaped with glass tube drawn into a long narrow stem. These used for the purpose of filtration.

(iv) Watch glass:- It is a flat dish made of glass. It is used for covering beakers or for preparation of solid mixtures or for taking small amounts of acids or sometimes used for evaporation of small quantities of liquids.

(v) Wire gauze:- It is a gauze made of fine iron wires fitted with a thin asbestos sheet in the centre. Glass apparatus are heated on wire gauze. This prevents the glass apparatus from cracking or breaking.

(vi) Tripod Stand:- It is made of cast iron and is used to hold a beaker or a flask over a flame.

(vii) Spatula:- It is a spoon made of nickel or steel. It is used for transferring small amount of solid substances.

(viii) Burners:- Burners are of different types. It is used for burning laboratory gas and producing flames.

(ix) Burette:- It is a long cylindrical graduated tube of uniform cross-section. The tube is fused with a stopcock at the lower end. Graduation is along from 0 to 50 ml from top to bottom. Each ml is again divided into 0.1 ml divisions.

(x) Pipette:- It is a handy glass apparatus for transferring a precise volume of liquid. It is a long narrow tube blown into a bulb at the middle. At the lower end it is drawn into a nozzle. At the upper end there is an etched mark. Pipettes are made of different capacities such as 10, 20, 25 ml etc.

(xi) Flat Bottomed Flask:- It is a glass bottle having a round body which is slightly flat at the bottom and a long narrow neck. It is used for storing solution and carrying out reactions in cold.

(xii) Round Bottomed Flask:- It is a flask consisting of a globe and narrow neck. It is made up of glass and is used for heating liquids.

(xiii) Specific Gravity Bottle:- Specific gravity bottles are used to find the liquid density. Measuring the liquids density. It is executed by finding the difference between emptied bottle and a filled bottle.

(xiv) Ostwald's Viscometer:- Ostwald viscometer also known as V-tube viscometer is used to measure the viscosity of the liquid with a known density. This device is named after “Wilhelm Ostwald”.

(xv) Stalagmometer:- A stalagmometer is a simple and commonly used instrument for measuring the surface tension (SFT) of liquids and most namely, the interfacial tension (IFT) between two liquids.

(xvi) Bunsen burner:- Device for combining a flammable gas with controlled amounts of air before ignition.

(xvii) Conical flask:- It is used to hold and measure chemical liquid sample.

(xviii) Measuring cylinder:- It is used to measure the approximate volume of different liquid.

(xix) Tongs:- It is an essential tools used for handling hot objects such as beakers, flask, or crucible. It help prevent burns and provide a secure grip when transferring or manipulating items in the lab.

(xx) Glass rod:- It is used to mix chemical and liquids for laboratory purposes.

(xxi) Volumetric flask:- It is used for the preparation and measurement of chemical solutions. It is put to use in the process of producing a solution at a predetermined volume.

(xxii) Burette stand:- It is used to hold and stabilize burette during titration or other laboratory purposes.

(xxiii) Dropper:- It is used to dispense small amounts of liquids medicines.

docs.title: Communication Process
docs.text: The communication process includes 6 main elements, that work together to share information effectively.

docs.title: Main Elements
docs.text:
1. Sender
  2. Message
  3. Channel
  4. Receiver
  5. Feedback
  6. Setting

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The person who starts the conversation to share an idea.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The sender creates a thought and adapts it to their tone to the listeners. A good communicator uses a polite, formal tone for elders or respected persons, and an easy, informal tone for friends or juniors.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A professor stands in front of the classroom to start a lecture on programming. Here, the professor is the sender.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The actual information, thought, or feeling being shared by the sender.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: It could be verbal (written or spoken words) or non-verbal (a friendly smile, a polite nod, or maintaining good eye contact). A proper message is always clear, respectful, and gentle.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
If I write a text like:

"Respected Sir, could you please guide me on the programming assignment?"

This polite request is the message.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The medium or path through which the message is forwarded from the sender to the receiver.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: It connects the speaker and the listener. It can be a formal channel like an official university email or letter, or an informal channel like a quick chat over social media or a face-to-face conversation.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A phone network used for calling a friend, or the air that carries my voice during a face-to-face conversation with my friend.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The person who gets the message and reads or listens to it.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The receiver breaks down the words to get the meaning. Proper behaviour means the receiver listens or reads patiently without interrupting, showing respect to the sender.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A student listening patiently and respectfully while their teacher delivers a lecture.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The reply or response sent back to the sender from the receiver.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: It completely finishes the communication cycle and proves the message was understood. Feedback can be verbal or non-verbal.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: When my mother explains an important topic to me, I listen carefully and nod my head to show that I've understood it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The physical place or situational environment where the communication takes place.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The location guides our behaviour. A classroom, library, or office creates a quiet, formal setting that requires strict politeness. A cafeteria, park, or hostel is a relaxed, informal setting.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: A well-arranged, quiet classroom with student benches, desks facing the teacher's blackboard creates a formal setting for a lecture.

docs.title: Communication Barriers
docs.text: A communication barrier is any obstacle that disrupts information, preventing the receiver from understanding the sender's intended message.

docs.title: 1. Language and Semantic Barriers
docs.text: Distortions caused by words, signs, symbols, or linguistic differences.

docs.title: Lack of Common Language
docs.text:
Communicating parties speak completely different languages.

Example: An Indian developer discussing code with a non-English-speaking international client.

docs.title: Semantics (Word Meaning)
docs.text:
Words that carry different meanings for different people.

Example: The word "bug" means an insect to a layman, but an error to a computer scientist.

docs.title: Vocabulary & Grammar
docs.text:
Poor sentence structure or punctuation changes the intended message.

Example: Wrongly placed commas in a configuration script that change system execution commands.

docs.title: Jargon
docs.text:
Using specialized, highly technical terms with non-technical people.

Example: Telling a client that your program uses an "asynchronous API microservice" instead of saying it is "fast and reliable."

docs.title: 2. Physical and Environmental Barriers
docs.text: Tangible or situational factors in the surrounding environment that block messages.

docs.title: Time Zone & Distance
docs.text:
Geographic gaps and time-zone differences that delay feedback.

Example: A tech team working in India trying to sync live with a manager in New York.

docs.title: Workspace Design and Noise
docs.text:
Disruptions caused by poor room layout or ambient sound.

Example: Conducting a team meeting next to a loud server room or on a dynamic factory floor.

docs.title: 3. Socio-Psychological Barriers
docs.text: Interferences caused by emotional states, social standing, and identity differences.

docs.title: Halo Effect
docs.text:
A cognitive bias where an overall impression of a person alters how you judge their specific traits.

Example: Thinking a candidate is highly organized and skilled just because they arrive at the interview well-dressed.

docs.title: Status Barrier
docs.text:
Workplace position or authority creates distance and intimidation between employees.

Example: A junior employee or student feeling too anxious to directly report a problem to the President or Principal.

docs.title: Different Perceptions of Reality
docs.text:
Interpreting the exact same situation differently based on your viewpoint.

Example: Two people looking at a multi-coloured object from different angles and disagreeing on its colour due to lighting.

docs.title: Distortion, Filtering and Editing
docs.text:
The systematic alteration of a message as it passes through multiple contact points.

Example: A game of "Chinese Whispers" where the final message is completely different from the original text.

docs.title: Past Experience
docs.text:
Previous life encounters and memories create biases that affect current communication.

Example: A negative past encounter with a stranger ruining someone's communication dynamic when they turn out to be your HOD.

docs.title: Poor Listening and Inattentiveness
docs.text:
Failing to process messages due to internal or external factors.

  • Internal factors: Hunger, fatigue, anger, or family issues.
  • External factors: Zoning out or choosing to ignore the speaker.

docs.title: 4. Organizational Barriers
docs.text: Obstacles tied directly to a company's structure, policy, or hierarchy.

docs.title: Key Causes
docs.text:
• Rigid top-down management structure
  • Complex communication channels
  • Restrictive policies

docs.title: Impact
docs.text:
Distort or block the flow of important workplace information.

Example: Frontline workers cannot answer customer tweets without legal team approval.

docs.title: 5. Cultural Barriers
docs.text:
Disruptions caused by geographic roots, regional settings, or background differences.

Example: Misunderstanding caused by varied regional accents or local dialects within the same language.

docs.title: 1. Fundamentals of Complex Numbers
docs.text:
• Definition: A number of the form \(z = a + ib\) where \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\) and \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) (iota).
  • Parts:
  • Real Part: \(\text{Re}(z) = a\)
  • Imaginary Part: \(\text{Im}(z) = b\)
  • Powers of Iota (\(i\)):
  • \(i = \sqrt{-1}\)
  • \(i^2 = -1\)
  • \(i^3 = -i\)
  • \(i^4 = 1\)

docs.title: 2. Basic Operations
docs.text:
For \(z_1 = a + ib\) and \(z_2 = c + id\):

  • Addition: \(z_1 + z_2 = (a+c) + i(b+d)\)
  • Subtraction: \(z_1 - z_2 = (a-c) + i(b-d)\)
  • Multiplication: \(z_1 \cdot z_2 = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc)\)
  • Division: \(\frac{z_1}{z_2} = \frac{(a+ib)(c-id)}{c^2+d^2} = \left(\frac{ac+bd}{c^2+d^2}\right) + i\left(\frac{bc-ad}{c^2+d^2}\right)\)
  • Equality: \(a + ib = x + iy \implies a = x\) and \(b = y\)

docs.title: 3. Conjugate, Modulus & Inverse
docs.text:
• Conjugate (\(\overline{z}\)):
  • If \(z = a + ib\), then \(\overline{z} = a - ib\).
  • Key Property: \(z \cdot \overline{z} = a^2 + b^2\)
  • Modulus (\(|z|\)):
  • \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\) (distance of \(z\) from origin in the Argand plane)
  • Multiplicative Inverse (\(z^{-1}\)):
  • \(z^{-1} = \frac{1}{z} = \frac{\overline{z}}{|z|^2} = \frac{a}{a^2+b^2} + i\left(\frac{-b}{a^2+b^2}\right)\)

docs.title: 4. Argument and Quadrant Rules
docs.text:
Reference angle: \(\alpha = \tan^{-1}\left|\frac{y}{x}\right|\)

Quadrant Location of \((x, y)\) Principal Argument (\(\theta\)) 1st Quadrant \(x > 0, y > 0\) \(\theta = \alpha\) 2nd Quadrant \(x < 0, y > 0\) \(\theta = 180^\circ - \alpha = \pi - \alpha\) 3rd Quadrant \(x < 0, y < 0\) \(\theta = -180^\circ + \alpha = -\pi + \alpha\) 4th Quadrant \(x > 0, y < 0\) \(\theta = -\alpha\)

docs.title: 5. Polar Form & De Moivre's Theorem
docs.text:
• Polar Form: \(z = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), where \(r = |z|\) and \(\theta = \text{arg}(z)\).
  • De Moivre's Theorem: For any integer \(n\): $\(z^n = [r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)]^n = r^n(\cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta)\)$

docs.title: 6. Square Root of a Complex Number
docs.text: To find \(\sqrt{x + iy} = a + ib\): 1. Square both sides: \(x + iy = (a^2 - b^2) + i(2ab)\) 2. Equate parts: \(a^2 - b^2 = x\) and \(2ab = y\) 3. Use identity: \(a^2 + b^2 = \sqrt{(a^2 - b^2)^2 + 4a^2b^2} = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) 4. Solve for \(a\) and \(b\), maintaining correct sign alignment from \(2ab\)

docs.title: Example:
docs.text:
Q. Find Square Root of: \(16-i30\)

\(sol^n\): Let, \(\sqrt{16-i30}=a+ib\)

Sqring both sides: \(\implies\) \(16-i30=(a+ib)^2\) \(\implies\) \(16-i30=(a^2-b^2)+i(2b)\)

By comparing LHS with RHS, We Get:

\(\implies\boxed{(a^2-b^2)=16}\rightarrow(1)\)

\(\implies\boxed{2b=30}\rightarrow(2)\)

By sqring and adding \((1)\) and \((2)\) ,

\((a^2-b^2)+(2b)^2=(16)^2+(30)^2\)

\(\implies(a^2+b^2)=256+900\)

\(\implies a^2+b^2=\sqrt{1156}\)

\(\implies \boxed{a^2+b^2=34}\rightarrow(3)\)

docs.title: 7. Solved Example Summary
docs.text: Problem Type Given Expression Result / Solution Simplification \(\frac{1+i}{1-i}\) \(0 + i(1) = i\) Multiplicative Inverse \(7 - 2i\) \(\frac{7}{53} + i\left(\frac{2}{53}\right)\) Square Root \(\sqrt{8 - 15i}\) \(\pm\left(\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} - i\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\right)\) Modulus & Argument \(1 + i\sqrt{3}\) \(r = 2\), \(\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}\ (60^\circ)\) De Moivre's Power \((1+i)^{16}\) \((\sqrt{2})^{16}(\cos 4\pi + i\sin 4\pi) = 256\)

docs.title: Comprehensive Notes on Partial Fraction Decomposition
1. Fundamental Definitions & Classifications
docs.text: A rational function (or rational fraction) is an expression of the form: $\(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\)$ where \(f(x)\) and \(g(x)\) are polynomials, with \(g(x) \neq 0\).

docs.title: A. Proper Fractions
docs.text:
A rational fraction \(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) is called a proper fraction if the degree of the numerator \(f(x)\) is strictly less than the degree of the denominator \(g(x)\): $\(\deg(f(x)) < \deg(g(x))\)$

  • Examples:
  • \(\frac{x}{x^2 + 4x + 4}\)
  • \(\frac{x}{x^2 + 1}\)

docs.title: B. Improper Fractions
docs.text:
A rational fraction \(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}\) is called an improper fraction if the degree of the numerator \(f(x)\) is greater than or equal to the degree of the denominator \(g(x)\): $\(\deg(f(x)) \ge \deg(g(x))\)$

  • Examples:
  • \(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x^2 + 3x + 2}\)
  • \(\frac{x^3 - 7x + 1}{x^3 + 2x^2 + 9}\)

Handling Improper Fractions: Prior to decomposing an improper fraction into partial fractions, perform polynomial long division to rewrite it as: $\(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = Q(x) + \frac{R(x)}{g(x)}\)$ where \(Q(x)\) is the quotient polynomial and \(\frac{R(x)}{g(x)}\) is a proper fraction (i.e., \(\deg(R(x)) < \deg(g(x))\)). Apply partial fraction decomposition to \(\frac{R(x)}{g(x)}\).

docs.title: Form:
docs.text: \[\frac{f(x)}{(ax + b)(cx + d)(ex + f)} = \frac{A}{ax + b} + \frac{B}{cx + d} + \frac{C}{ex + f}\]

docs.title: Example 1: Two Distinct Linear Factors
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x}{(x+1)(x-2)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the partial fraction equation: $\(\frac{x}{(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{x-2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Combine terms over a common denominator: $\(\frac{x}{(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{A(x-2) + B(x+1)}{(x+1)(x-2)}\)$

  2. Equate the numerators: $\(A(x-2) + B(x+1) = x \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  3. Solve for constants by substitution:

  4. Set \(x = 2\) in (2): $\(A(0) + B(2+1) = 2 \implies 3B = 2 \implies B = \frac{2}{3}\)$

  5. Set \(x = -1\) in (2): $\(A(-1-2) + B(0) = -1 \implies -3A = -1 \implies A = \frac{1}{3}\)$

  6. Substitute constants back into (1): $\(\frac{x}{(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{1/3}{x+1} + \frac{2/3}{x-2}\)$

docs.title: Example 2: Three Distinct Linear Factors
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x+2)(x-3)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the equation: $\(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x+2)(x-3)} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{x+2} + \frac{C}{x-3} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(x+2)(x-3) + B(x+1)(x-3) + C(x+1)(x+2) = x^2 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Solve for constants:

  3. Set \(x = -1\): $\(A(-1+2)(-1-3) = (-1)^2 \implies A(1)(-4) = 1 \implies -4A = 1 \implies A = -\frac{1}{4}\)$
  4. Set \(x = -2\): $\(B(-2+1)(-2-3) = (-2)^2 \implies B(-1)(-5) = 4 \implies 5B = 4 \implies B = \frac{4}{5}\)$

  5. Set \(x = 3\): $\(C(3+1)(3+2) = (3)^2 \implies C(4)(5) = 9 \implies 20C = 9 \implies C = \frac{9}{20}\)$

  6. Final decomposition: $\(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x+2)(x-3)} = \frac{-1/4}{x+1} + \frac{4/5}{x+2} + \frac{9/20}{x-3}\)$

docs.title: Example 3: Three Factors including a Monomial Factor
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x(x+1)(x-2)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the decomposition: $\(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{A}{x} + \frac{B}{x+1} + \frac{C}{x-2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(x+1)(x-2) + Bx(x-2) + Cx(x+1) = x^2 + 1 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Solve for constants:

  3. Set \(x = 0\): $\(A(1)(-2) = 0^2 + 1 \implies -2A = 1 \implies A = -\frac{1}{2}\)$
  4. Set \(x = -1\): $\(B(-1)(-1-2) = (-1)^2 + 1 \implies 3B = 2 \implies B = \frac{2}{3}\)$

  5. Set \(x = 2\): $\(C(2)(2+1) = 2^2 + 1 \implies 6C = 5 \implies C = \frac{5}{6}\)$

  6. Final decomposition: $\(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{-1/2}{x} + \frac{2/3}{x+1} + \frac{5/6}{x-2}\)$

docs.title: Example 4: General Symbolic Formula
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{1}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the expansion: $\(\frac{1}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{B}{x-b} + \frac{C}{x-c}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(x-b)(x-c) + B(x-a)(x-c) + C(x-a)(x-b) = 1\)$

  2. Evaluate at roots:

  3. Set \(x = a\): \(A(a-b)(a-c) = 1 \implies A = \frac{1}{(a-b)(a-c)}\)
  4. Set \(x = b\): \(B(b-a)(b-c) = 1 \implies B = \frac{1}{(b-a)(b-c)}\)

  5. Set \(x = c\): \(C(c-a)(c-b) = 1 \implies C = \frac{1}{(c-a)(c-b)}\)

  6. Final Result: $\(\frac{1}{(x-a)(x-b)(x-c)} = \frac{1}{(a-b)(a-c)(x-a)} + \frac{1}{(b-a)(b-c)(x-b)} + \frac{1}{(c-a)(c-b)(x-c)}\)$

docs.title: Type II: Improper Fractions with Non-Repeated Linear Factors
Method:
docs.text: Divide the numerator by the denominator using long division first to separate the polynomial part, then perform partial fraction decomposition on the remainder fraction.

docs.title: Example 1:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{4x^2 + 1}{(2x+1)(x+2)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Expand the denominator: $\((2x+1)(x+2) = 2x^2 + 5x + 2\)$

  1. Perform Long Division: Divide \((4x^2 + 1)\) by \((2x^2 + 5x + 2)\): $\(\frac{4x^2 + 1}{2x^2 + 5x + 2} = 2 + \frac{-10x - 3}{2x^2 + 5x + 2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  2. Decompose the remainder fraction: $\(\frac{-10x - 3}{(2x+1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{2x+1} + \frac{B}{x+2}\)$ $\(A(x+2) + B(2x+1) = -10x - 3 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  3. Solve for constants:

  4. Set \(x = -2\): $\(B(2(-2) + 1) = -10(-2) - 3 \implies -3B = 17 \implies B = -\frac{17}{3}\)$

  5. Set \(x = -\frac{1}{2}\): $\(A\left(-\frac{1}{2} + 2\right) = -10\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) - 3 \implies \frac{3}{2}A = 2 \implies A = \frac{4}{3}\)$

  6. Substitute back into (1): $\(\frac{4x^2 + 1}{(2x+1)(x+2)} = 2 + \frac{4/3}{2x+1} - \frac{17/3}{x+2}\)$

docs.title: Example 2:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^3 + 7x + 1}{x^2 + 5x + 6}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Perform Long Division: $\(\frac{x^3 + 7x + 1}{x^2 + 5x + 6} = x - 5 + \frac{26x + 31}{x^2 + 5x + 6} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Factor denominator and set up partial fractions for the remainder: $\(\frac{26x + 31}{(x+2)(x+3)} = \frac{A}{x+2} + \frac{B}{x+3}\)$ $\(A(x+3) + B(x+2) = 26x + 31 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Solve for constants:

  3. Set \(x = -2\): $\(A(-2+3) = 26(-2) + 31 \implies A = -21\)$

  4. Set \(x = -3\): $\(B(-3+2) = 26(-3) + 31 \implies -B = -47 \implies B = 47\)$

  5. Final Result: $\(\frac{x^3 + 7x + 1}{x^2 + 5x + 6} = x - 5 - \frac{21}{x+2} + \frac{47}{x+3}\)$

docs.title: Example 3:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2}{(3x+2)(2x+3)}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Expand denominator: $\((3x+2)(2x+3) = 6x^2 + 13x + 6\)$

  1. Perform Long Division: $\(\frac{x^2}{6x^2 + 13x + 6} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{-\frac{13}{6}x - 1}{6x^2 + 13x + 6} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  2. Decompose the remainder fraction: $\(\frac{-\frac{13}{6}x - 1}{(3x+2)(2x+3)} = \frac{A}{3x+2} + \frac{B}{2x+3}\)$ $\(A(2x+3) + B(3x+2) = -\frac{13}{6}x - 1 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  3. Solve for constants:

  4. Set \(x = -\frac{2}{3}\): $\(A\left(2\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)+3\right) = -\frac{13}{6}\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)-1 \implies \frac{5}{3}A = \frac{4}{9} \implies A = \frac{1}{3}\)$

  5. Set \(x = -\frac{3}{2}\): $\(B\left(3\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)+2\right) = -\frac{13}{6}\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)-1 \implies -\frac{5}{2}B = \frac{9}{4} \implies B = -\frac{9}{10}\)$

  6. Final Result: $\(\frac{x^2}{(3x+2)(2x+3)} = \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1/3}{3x+2} - \frac{9/10}{2x+3}\)$

docs.title: Form:
docs.text:
If \(g(x) = (ax + b)(cx + d)^n\), assume: $\(\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{A}{ax + b} + \frac{B}{cx + d} + \frac{C}{(cx + d)^2} + \dots + \frac{Z}{(cx + d)^n}\)$

Note: Direct substitution alone is usually insufficient to determine all constants in repeated factor cases. Combine substitution with equating coefficients of like powers of \(x\).

docs.title: Example 1:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x-1)^2}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the equation: $\(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x-1)^2} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{x-1} + \frac{C}{(x-1)^2} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(x-1)^2 + B(x+1)(x-1) + C(x+1) = x^2 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Find constants:

  3. Set \(x = 1\) in (2): $\(C(1+1) = 1^2 \implies 2C = 1 \implies C = \frac{1}{2}\)$

  4. Set \(x = -1\) in (2): $\(A(-1-1)^2 = (-1)^2 \implies 4A = 1 \implies A = \frac{1}{4}\)$

  5. Expand terms in (2) to solve for \(B\): $\(A(x^2 - 2x + 1) + B(x^2 - 1) + C(x + 1) = x^2\)$ $\((A + B)x^2 + (-2A + C)x + (A - B + C) = x^2\)$

  6. Equate coefficients of \(x^2\): $\(A + B = 1 \implies \frac{1}{4} + B = 1 \implies B = \frac{3}{4}\)$

  7. Final Result: $\(\frac{x^2}{(x+1)(x-1)^2} = \frac{1/4}{x+1} + \frac{3/4}{x-1} + \frac{1/2}{(x-1)^2}\)$

docs.title: Example 2:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2 + 4x + 1}{(1-x)^4}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the equation: $\(\frac{x^2 + 4x + 1}{(1-x)^4} = \frac{A}{1-x} + \frac{B}{(1-x)^2} + \frac{C}{(1-x)^3} + \frac{D}{(1-x)^4} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(1-x)^3 + B(1-x)^2 + C(1-x) + D = x^2 + 4x + 1 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Solve for \(D\):

  3. Set \(x = 1\): $\(D = 1^2 + 4(1) + 1 = 6\)$

  4. Expand polynomial terms to find \(A, B, C\): $\(A(1 - 3x + 3x^2 - x^3) + B(1 - 2x + x^2) + C(1 - x) + D = x^2 + 4x + 1\)$ $\((-A)x^3 + (3A + B)x^2 + (-3A - 2B - C)x + (A + B + C + D) = x^2 + 4x + 1\)$

  5. Equate coefficients of like powers:

  6. Coefficient of \(x^3\): $\(-A = 0 \implies A = 0\)$
  7. Coefficient of \(x^2\): $\(3A + B = 1 \implies 3(0) + B = 1 \implies B = 1\)$

  8. Coefficient of \(x\): $\(-3A - 2B - C = 4 \implies -3(0) - 2(1) - C = 4 \implies -2 - C = 4 \implies C = -6\)$

  9. Final Result: $\(\frac{x^2 + 4x + 1}{(1-x)^4} = \frac{1}{(1-x)^2} - \frac{6}{(1-x)^3} + \frac{6}{(1-x)^4}\)$

docs.title: Example 3:
docs.text:
Resolve \(\frac{x^2 + 2x + 3}{(x+1)^3}\) into partial fractions.

Solution: 1. Set up the expansion: $\(\frac{x^2 + 2x + 3}{(x+1)^3} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{(x+1)^2} + \frac{C}{(x+1)^3} \quad \text{--- (1)}\)$

  1. Equate numerators: $\(A(x+1)^2 + B(x+1) + C = x^2 + 2x + 3 \quad \text{--- (2)}\)$

  2. Find constants:

  3. Set \(x = -1\): $\(C = (-1)^2 + 2(-1) + 3 = 1 - 2 + 3 = 2\)$
  4. Expand (2): $\(A(x^2 + 2x + 1) + B(x + 1) + C = x^2 + 2x + 3\)$ $\(Ax^2 + (2A + B)x + (A + B + C) = x^2 + 2x + 3\)$
  5. Equate coefficient of \(x^2\): $\(A = 1\)$

  6. Equate coefficient of \(x\): $\(2A + B = 2 \implies 2(1) + B = 2 \implies B = 0\)$

  7. Verification: $\(\text{RHS} = \frac{1}{x+1} + \frac{2}{(x+1)^3} = \frac{(x+1)^2 + 2}{(x+1)^3} = \frac{x^2 + 2x + 1 + 2}{(x+1)^3} = \frac{x^2 + 2x + 3}{(x+1)^3} \quad \text{(Matches LHS)}\)$

  8. Final Result: $\(\frac{x^2 + 2x + 3}{(x+1)^3} = \frac{1}{x+1} + \frac{2}{(x+1)^3}\)$

docs.title: Form:
docs.text: If \(g(x)\) contains an irreducible quadratic factor \(bx^2 + cx + d\) (i.e. cannot be factored into real linear factors), assign a linear numerator \(Bx + C\): $\(\frac{f(x)}{(x+a)(bx^2 + cx + d)} = \frac{A}{x+a} + \frac{Bx + C}{bx^2 + cx + d}\)$

docs.title: 3. General Step-by-Step Problem Solving Strategy
docs.text:
1. Check Fraction Type: Compare \(\deg(f(x))\) and \(\deg(g(x))\). If \(\deg(f(x)) \ge \deg(g(x))\), perform long division first.
  2. Factor Denominator: Factor \(g(x)\) completely into linear and irreducible quadratic factors.
  3. Set Up Partial Fraction Expression:
  4. Linear factor \((ax+b) \implies \frac{A}{ax+b}\)
  5. Repeated linear factor \((ax+b)^n \implies \frac{A_1}{ax+b} + \frac{A_2}{(ax+b)^2} + \dots + \frac{A_n}{(ax+b)^n}\)
  6. Irreducible quadratic factor \((ax^2+bx+c) \implies \frac{Ax+B}{ax^2+bx+c}\)
  7. Form Algebraic Equation: Multiply through by \(g(x)\) to clear all denominators.
  8. Solve for Unknown Constants:
  9. Substitute roots of linear factors to isolate constants directly.
  10. Expand terms and equate coefficients of corresponding powers of \(x\) to solve remaining linear systems.

docs.title: Elasticity
docs.text: The property by virtue of which if a material is deformed under the application of external force, after removing the external force, the internal restoring force bring back the body to its original configuration is known as elasticity.

docs.title: Stress
docs.text:
If a body is deformed by an external force, the body can get its original configuration by the help of the internal restoring force after the removal of external, one.

This restoring force per unit area is known as stress.

\[ \text{Stress}=\frac{\text{restoring force}}{\text{area}}=\frac{F}{A} \] \[ =\frac{N}{m^2} \] \[ = \left[\frac{N}{m^2}\right] = \left[\frac{MLT^{-2}}{L^2}\right] \] \[ =\left[ML^{-1}T^{-2}\right] \]

Unit: \(N.m^{-2}\)

docs.title: Strain
docs.text:
If an elastic body is deformed by an application of external force, the ratio of deformation to its original config. is known as strain.

Let it is unit less and dimensionless quantity.

Let,

  • deformation be \(L_2\)
  • original config. be \(L_1\)
\[ \text{Strain} = \frac{\text{change in config.}} {\text{original config.}} \]

docs.title: Longitudinal strain
docs.text: \[ \text{Longitudinal strain} = \frac{\text{change in length }(\Delta L)} {\text{original length }(L)} \]

docs.title: Volumetric Strain
docs.text: \[ \text{Volumetric strain} = \frac{\text{change in volume }(\Delta V)} {\text{original volume }(V)} \]

docs.title: Shearing Strain
docs.text: \[ \text{Shearing strain} = \text{ Angular Change } \space \theta  \]

docs.title: Hook's Law
docs.text:
It states that under elastic limits, stress of a body is directly proportional to its strain.

i.e.

\[ \boxed{\text{Stress}\propto\text{strain}} \]

or,

\[ \boxed{\text{stress}=(\text{constant})\times\text{strain}} \]

The constant of proportionality is known as co-efficient of elasticity or modulus of elastic elasticity.

\[ \boxed{ \text{modulus of elasticity} = \frac{\text{stress}}{\text{strain}} } \]

docs.title: Unit and Dimension of Modulus of Elasticity
docs.text:
The unit of and dimension of modulus of elasticity is, similar to that of stress.

i.e.

\[ N.m^{-2} \] \[ [ML^{-1}T^{-2}] \]

respectively.

docs.title: 1. Young's Modulus (for longitudinal strain)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{ \text{Young's Modulus} = \frac{\text{Normal stress}} {\text{longi. strain}} } \]

or

\[ \boxed{ Y= \frac{F/A}{\Delta L/L} } \]

docs.title: 2. Bulk Modulus (for volumetric strain)
docs.text: \[ \boxed{ \text{Bulk Modulus} = \frac{\text{Normal stress}} {\text{Volumetric strain}} } \] \[ \boxed{ K\text{ or }B= \frac{F/A}{\Delta V/V} } \]

docs.title: 3. Shearing Modulus (for shearing strain)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{ \text{Shearing Modulus} = \frac{\text{Shearing stress}} {\text{Shearing strain}} } \]

or

\[ \boxed{ \eta= \frac{F/A}{\theta} } \]

docs.title: Q. A string of 60 cm long is stretched by 2 cm by the application of load 200 gm. What will be the length when a load of 500 gm is applied?
Soln.
docs.text:
Given,

Original length of string \(=60cm\)

By load of 200gm

If load \(=200gm\)

then,

\[ \text{Str. stretched}=2cm \]

By using Hook's law,

\[ \frac{E_1}{W_1} = \frac{E_2}{W_2} \]

1)

\[ \frac{2}{200} = \frac{E_2}{500} \] \[ E_2 = \frac{2\times500}{200} \] \[ E_2=5cm \]

Hence,

the new length will be

\[ =5+60cm \] \[ =65cm \]

docs.title: 1st case
docs.text:
\[ mg=\frac{200}{1000}\times9.8 = 0.2\times9.8 \] \[ \Delta L=2cm = \frac{2}{100}m = 2\times10^{-2} = 0.02m \]

Let \(A\) be the area of cross of section of the string.

and \(Y\) as the i.e. the co-efficient of elasticity of the material.

\[ Y= \frac{mg\times g\times L}{A(\Delta L)} \] \[ = \frac{0.2\times9.8\times0.6} {A(0.02)} \qquad -(1) \]

docs.title: In 2nd case the applied load is 500gm
docs.text:
Thus,

\[ Y = \frac{0.5\times9.8\times0.6} {A(\Delta L_2)} \qquad -(2) \]

\(Y\) remains same in both situation.

So,

\[ (1)=(2) \] \[ \frac{0.2\times9.8\times0.6} {A(0.02)} = \frac{0.5\times9.8\times0.6} {A(\Delta L_2)} \]

i)

\[ \frac{0.2}{0.02} = \frac{0.5}{\Delta L_2} \] \[ \Delta L_2 = \frac{0.02\times0.5}{0.2} \] \[ =5\times10^{-2} \] \[ =0.05m \] \[ =5cm \]

Hence,

\[ \text{new }L=L+\Delta L_2 \] \[ =60+5 \] \[ \boxed{=65cm} \]

docs.title: Q. The Young's Modulus of steel \(2\times10^{11}N.m^{-2}\)
Q.
docs.text: The Young's Modulus for steel \(2\times10^{11}N.m^{-2}\) is the inter atomic spacing of material is \(2.8\). Find the increasing inter atomic spacing for the stress of \(10^9N.m^{-2} Å\)

docs.title: Soln.
docs.text:
Force

\[ Y=2\times10^{11}N.m^{-2} \] \[ L=2.8 Å = 2.8\times10^{-10}m \] \[ =28\times10^{-11}m \]

Stress

\[ = \frac{F}{A} = 10^9N.m^{-2} \]

We know that

\[ Y= \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} \]

or,

\[ \text{Strain} = \frac{\text{Stress}}{Y} \] \[ \frac{\Delta L}{L} = \frac{\text{Stress}}{Y} \] \[ = \Delta L = \frac{\text{Stress}}{Y}\times L \] \[ \frac{10^9\times28\times10^{-11}} {2\times10^{11}} \] \[ \Delta L = 14\times10^{9-11-11} \] \[ = 14\times10^{9-22} \] \[ = 14\times10^{-13}m \] \[ = 0.014 Å \]

The Poisson's Ratio always stays between \(0\) & \(1\).

docs.title: 1. Force
docs.text:
Force is defined as:

\[ F = ma \]

where:

  • \(F\) = force
  • \(m\) = mass
  • \(a\) = acceleration

The SI unit of force is Newton (N).

docs.title: Four Fundamental Forces
docs.text:
1. Gravitational force
  2. Electromagnetic force
  3. Strong nuclear force
  4. Weak nuclear force

docs.title: 2. Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
docs.text:
Newton's law of gravitation states:

Every two bodies in the universe attract each other with a force that is directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

For two bodies of masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\), separated by distance \(r\):

\[ F \propto m_1m_2 \]

and

\[ F \propto \frac{1}{r^2} \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{F = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2}} \]

where \(G\) is the universal gravitational constant.

docs.title: Value of \(G\)
docs.text:
\[ \boxed{G = 6.674\times10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\text{kg}^{-2}} \]

\(G\) is universal, meaning its value is the same everywhere.

docs.title: 3. Gravitational Constant \(G\)
docs.text:
From

\[ F = G\frac{m_1m_2}{r^2} \]

we get

\[ \boxed{G=\frac{Fr^2}{m_1m_2}} \]

The gravitational constant is defined as the gravitational force between two bodies of unit mass separated by unit distance.

docs.title: 4. Relation Between \(g\) and \(G\)
docs.text:
Consider a body of mass \(m\) near the surface of Earth.

Let:

  • \(M_E\) = mass of Earth
  • \(R_E\) = radius of Earth
  • \(m\) = mass of the body
  • \(g\) = acceleration due to gravity

The force on the body due to gravity is:

\[ F_1 = mg \]

From Newton's law of gravitation:

\[ F_2 = G\frac{M_E m}{R_E^2} \]

Since both expressions represent the same gravitational force:

\[ mg = G\frac{M_E m}{R_E^2} \]

Cancel \(m\):

\[ \boxed{g = G\frac{M_E}{R_E^2}} \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{g=\frac{GM_E}{R_E^2}} \]

docs.title: 5. Acceleration Due to Gravity
docs.text:
The acceleration due to gravity is approximately:

\[ \boxed{g=9.8\ \text{m/s}^2} \]

docs.title: Dimensional Formula
docs.text:
\[ g = \frac{\text{length}}{\text{time}^2} \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{[g]=[LT^{-2}]} \]

docs.title: 6. Weight of a Body
docs.text:
Weight is the gravitational force exerted by Earth on a body.

\[ \boxed{W=mg} \]

where:

  • \(W\) = weight
  • \(m\) = mass
  • \(g\) = acceleration due to gravity

The SI unit of weight is Newton (N).

docs.title: 9. Acceleration Due to Gravity on the Moon
Question
docs.text:
What will be the acceleration due to gravity on the Moon if:

  • Radius of Moon = \(\frac14\) radius of Earth
  • Mass of Moon = \(\frac1{80}\) mass of Earth

docs.title: Given
docs.text:
\[ R_M=\frac{R_E}{4} \] \[ M_M=\frac{M_E}{80} \]

We know:

\[ g=G\frac{M}{R^2} \]

For Earth:

\[ g_E=G\frac{M_E}{R_E^2} \]

For Moon:

\[ g_M=G\frac{M_M}{R_M^2} \]

Therefore,

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{g_M}{g_E} &= \frac{M_M}{M_E} \frac{R_E^2}{R_M^2} \end{aligned} \]

Substituting:

\[ \begin{aligned} \frac{g_M}{g_E} &= \frac1{80} \left(\frac{R_E}{R_E/4}\right)^2 \\ &= \frac1{80}(4)^2 \\ &= \frac{16}{80} \\ &= \frac15 \end{aligned} \]

Hence,

\[ g_M=\frac{g_E}{5} \]

Taking \(g_E=9.8\,\text{m/s}^2\):

\[ g_M=\frac{9.8}{5} \] \[ \boxed{g_M=1.96\ \text{m/s}^2} \]

docs.title: 11. Gravitational Force Between an Electron and a Proton
Question
docs.text: Find the gravitational force between an electron and a proton if their separation is \(1\,\text{A}\).

docs.title: Given
docs.text:
Mass of electron:

\[ m_e=9.1\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg} \]

Mass of proton:

\[ m_p=1.67\times10^{-27}\,\text{kg} \]

Separation:

\[ r=1\,\text{A} \]

Since:

\[ 1\,\text{A}=10^{-10}\,\text{m} \]

we have:

\[ r=10^{-10}\,\text{m} \]

Using:

\[ F=G\frac{m_em_p}{r^2} \] \[ F= \frac{ (6.67\times10^{-11}) (9.1\times10^{-31}) (1.67\times10^{-27}) }{ (10^{-10})^2 } \]

Therefore,

\[ \boxed{F\approx1.014\times10^{-47}\ \text{N}} \]

docs.text: Diploma / Sem I / DMA101 (Midterm) 2026 ENGINEERING MATHEMATICS II Full Marks: 50 Time: Two (2) hours The figures in the margin indicate full marks for the questions. Answer any five (5) questions.

• a) If \(\sin \theta = \frac{4}{5}\), find the value of \(\frac{4 \tan \theta - 5 \cos \theta}{\sec \theta + 4 \cot \theta}\) (5)
  • b) Evaluate (any two): (\(2.5 \times 2 = 5\))
    • (i) \(\sin 30^\circ \cos 45^\circ + \cos 30^\circ \sin 45^\circ\)
    • (ii) \(\tan 30^\circ \sec 45^\circ + \tan 60^\circ \sec 30^\circ\)
    • (iii) \(\tan 60^\circ \tan 45^\circ + \tan 60^\circ \tan 45^\circ\)

• a) Show that (any two): (\(2.5 \times 2 = 5\))

    • (i) \(\frac{\sin A + \sin B}{\cos A + \cos B} = \tan \frac{A + B}{2}\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{\sin A + \sin B}{\cos B - \cos A} = \cot \frac{A + B}{2} \cot \frac{A - B}{2}\)
    • (iii) \(\sin 20^\circ \sin 40^\circ \sin 60^\circ \sin 80^\circ = \frac{1}{16}\)

  • b) Prove that (any two): (\(2.5 \times 2 = 5\))

    • (i) \(\frac{\cot A - \tan A}{\cot A + \tan A} = \cos 2A\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{\sin A + \sin 2A}{1 + \cos A + \cos 2A} = \tan A\)
    • (iii) \(\frac{\cos A - \sin A}{\cos A + \sin A} = \sec 2A - \tan 2A\)

• a) Express the following in the form of \(A + iB\) (any one): (5)

    • (i) \(\frac{3 + 2i}{4 - 5i} + \frac{3 - 2i}{4 + 5i}\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{(3 - 2i)(2 + 3i)}{(1 + 2i)(2 - i)}\)

  • b) If \(x = 3 + 2i\) and \(y = 3 - 2i\), then find the values of \(x^3 + y^3\). (5)

• a) If \(x + iy = \frac{a + ib}{a - ib}\), then show that \(x^2 + y^2 = 1\). (6)

  • b) Find the square root of the following (any one): (4)

    • (i) \(16 - 30i\)
    • (ii) \(-8 + 6i\)
    • (iii) \(-i\)

• a) Find the conjugate of the following (any one): (5)

    • (i) \(\frac{1 + 3i}{5 - 4i} + \frac{2 - 3i}{5 + 4i}\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{(1 + 2i)(2 - i)}{(3 - 2i)(2 + 3i)}\)

  • b) Use De-Moivre's theorem to compute the following (any one): (5)

    • (i) \((\sqrt{3} + 3i)^6\)
    • (ii) \((-\sqrt{2} + i\sqrt{2})^6\)

• a) For what real values of \(x\) and \(y\) are the complex numbers \(-3 + ix^2y\) and \(x^2 + y + 4i\) conjugate of each other? (5)

  • b) Resolve the following into partial fractions (any one): (5)

    • (i) \(\frac{7x - 1}{6x^2 - 5x + 1}\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{x^2 + 1}{x(x^2 - 1)}\)

• a) Resolve the following into partial fractions (any one): (10)
    • (i) \(\frac{x^2 + 3}{x^3(x + 3)}\)
    • (ii) \(\frac{x^2 - 2}{(x^2 + 3x)(x^2 + 2)}\)
